solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Small dog circling large seal

indicators.note: to circle something is to go right round it, so the dog's letters surround the L

blocks.note: a pug is a small snub-nosed dog; it opens round the rest
L = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A little dog running rings round a big seal on a beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seal' sits there as the animal to go with the dog; it is the verb or noun for a stopper.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the stopper in a sink or barrel closes it off tight, which is what a seal does.

clue.text: Poet catching the second reptile

indicators.note: LEAR holds THE inside him

blocks.note: Edward Lear, the nonsense poet; he wraps round THE
as printed
to second a motion is to back it

explanation.surface: A poet grabbing hold of some reptile or other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a number or a unit of time; it is the verb, to support.
explanation.definitionFit: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle, and turtles are reptiles.

clue.text: Crowd quiet on long thin dock platform

blocks.note: a gang = a crowd, a group
p = piano, quiet in music
lank = long and thin, as of hair or a person

explanation.surface: Dockers told to keep it down while standing on a narrow jetty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' looks like an adjective for the crowd; it is the musical direction piano, shortened to P.
explanation.definitionFit: A gangplank is the board laid from a ship to the dock for boarding.

clue.text: Island stocking much drink for venue hosting big game?

indicators.note: SARK stocks, i.e. holds, the other pieces

blocks.note: Sark is one of the Channel Islands; it goes round the rest
far better = much better
IPA = India pale ale, a beer

explanation.surface: An island bar stocked with plenty of booze for a big match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big game' reads as a major sporting fixture; the question mark flags the other sense, large wild animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari park keeps lions, elephants and the like, the big game of hunting.

clue.text: Character upset bearing back and front part of chest

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the letters upside down, so they read backwards
UM carries STERN above it in the column

blocks.note: the stern is the back of a ship
mu, a Greek letter, turned up to give UM

explanation.surface: Someone with a bad back also suffering chest pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' and 'chest' look like two bits of anatomy; the back belongs to a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The anatomical name for the breastbone, the flat bone down the middle of the ribcage's front.

clue.text: Amusing builder outside supermarket run for parlour boss?

indicators.note: ERECTOR goes outside ALDI and R

blocks.note: fun = amusing
one who erects, a builder; it wraps round the next two
Aldi, the discount supermarket chain
r = run, as on a cricket scoreboard

explanation.surface: A jokey builder dashing out of the shops to run a café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parlour' suggests an ice-cream or beauty parlour; the question mark points to a funeral parlour.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint: an undertaker's premises are called a funeral parlour, and the undertaker in charge runs it.

clue.text: What’s left on uniform team adopts

indicators.note: SIDE takes U in, as a family takes in a child

blocks.note: re = on, concerning
a side = a team; it holds the U
U is Uniform in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A team taking on a new kit, with the old uniform left over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like kit for the team; it is only the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: A residue is what remains after the rest has gone.

clue.text: Element of legalese possibly ignored by judge

indicators.note: the judge's letter J is left out

blocks.note: legalese is an example of jargon, hence 'possibly'
J = judge, dropped from the front

explanation.surface: A judge skipping the tricky legal wording of a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element of legalese' reads as a part of legal language; the definition is just 'Element', a chemical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a chemical element, a noble gas.

clue.text: Stick cut of reared beef in kitchen

indicators.note: the answer is a cut, a slice, taken from the words that follow
in a down clue, reared means standing up, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: the letters sit across beEF IN Kitchen and are read from the bottom up

explanation.surface: A butcher's cut of beef raised on the farm, served in a kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' pairs naturally with a beef joint as a noun; it is the verb, to stab.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick someone is to stab them, which is to knife them.

clue.text: Serving game or possibly swan in Lent

indicators.note: the letters are one possible arrangement of another set

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Whether to serve game birds or swan during Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serving game' reads like a dish of pheasant on a menu; the serving is the tennis stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn tennis is the full name of tennis, a game where each point starts with a serve.

clue.text: Put gold periodically in front of one cross

indicators.note: every other letter is taken
to be in front of is to come first, so these letters lead and the I follows

blocks.note: pUt GoLd, the even letters
I = one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Placing gold ahead of a cross, as on a medal or crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like the shape or an angry mood; here it is a hybrid.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a cross of grapefruit, orange and tangerine.

clue.text: Interrupt primate delivering Mass at home

indicators.note: delivering up the M, so it is given away and removed

blocks.note: CHIMP without M (mass)
in = at home

explanation.surface: A chimp saying Mass in someone's living room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' could be an archbishop, which fits Mass; it is the ape.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to chip in means to add a remark while others are talking, cutting across them.

clue.text: Beaming adult in row visiting Derby?

definitions.note: 'Beaming' as a noun, the act of glowing

indicators.note: 'adult in row' puts the adult's letter inside the row's letters
a visitor goes inside the place visited, so the row enters the race

blocks.note: the Derby is a famous horse race at Epsom; it wraps round the rest
a row is a din, a noise; it holds the A
A = adult, the film certificate

explanation.surface: A grinning grown-up caught in a squabble at the races.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is the premier English flat horse race, hence the question mark for a race by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiance is a glowing brightness, the quality of beaming.

clue.text: One vocally rouses singer broken by English article

indicators.note: CHER is split open by the E

blocks.note: Cher, the American singer
E = English
a leader is a newspaper's main opinion article

explanation.surface: A pop star's show being interrupted by an English newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like the grammatical kind (a, the); it is a newspaper editorial, called a leader in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheerleader rouses a crowd by shouting and chanting.

clue.text: Hunter from Med destination avoided by crew

indicators.note: the crew's letters are kept out of the island's name

blocks.note: Menorca, a Balearic island and holiday spot
a crew is its men; they are dropped from the front

explanation.surface: A killer whale in the Mediterranean that sailors steer clear of.
explanation.walkthrough: The island is spelt the Spanish way, Menorca, rather than Minorca.
explanation.definitionFit: The orca, or killer whale, is an apex predator that hunts seals and fish.

clue.text: Maidens poorly record nameless garden’s creatures

indicators.note: less the N, the abbreviation for name

blocks.note: M = maiden (over), from cricket scoring
poorly = ill
an EP is an extended-play record
EDEN'S without N (name)

explanation.surface: Sickly young women keeping a log of the bugs in an anonymous garden.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden is a cricket over with no runs scored, M on the scorecard. 'Garden's creatures' reads as the definition, but the garden is EDEN in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A general term for an example: millepedes (a variant spelling of millipedes) are many-legged creatures.

clue.text: Cycling charts originally in study happily found

indicators.note: the letters go round in a cycle, the last two moving to the front
originally = at the start, so each first letter is used

blocks.note: tables = charts; cycled to ESTABL
In Study Happily, the first letters

explanation.surface: A student glad to discover some cycling charts in the study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the past tense of find; it is the verb to found, to set up.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of setting something up for the first time, as with a college or a firm.

clue.text: Endure visit arranged by tense protestor

indicators.note: the letters of VISIT are put in a new order

blocks.note: to hack it = to endure, cope
anagram fodder, rearranged
t = tense, the grammar abbreviation

explanation.surface: Putting up with a visit set up by an edgy demonstrator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for the protestor; it is the grammatical term.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacktivist protests by hacking computer systems.

clue.text: Fancy English and French friend returning full of spirit

indicators.note: E and AMI turn back, going up the column
the reversed letters are filled with GIN

blocks.note: E = English
ami is French for friend
gin, a spirit, goes inside

explanation.surface: An Englishman and his French pal coming home tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective; it is the verb, as in 'Fancy that!'
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the old sense of fancy, to picture in the mind, as in 'Fancy meeting you here!'

clue.text: Means of access in cargo area below tug declared

indicators.note: said out loud, so the sound gives the letters
HOLD sits under TOE in the column

blocks.note: to tow is to tug, spoken as toe
a ship's hold carries its cargo

explanation.surface: A tugboat and its cargo hold, with docking announced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Means of access' sounds like a door or gangway; it is a foothold, a small first grip.
explanation.definitionFit: A toehold is a small initial position from which to gain entry or advance.

clue.text: Rent out of bounds outlets

indicators.note: the bounds, the outer letters, are removed

blocks.note: retail outlets = stores; its first and last letters go

explanation.surface: Rent being charged for shops in an off-limits area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid for property; it is the past tense of rend.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent is the past tense of rend, to tear, so rent = tore.

clue.text: Panic about a lot of good cosmetic use

indicators.note: about = round the outside of, so the panic's letters surround the rest
most, but not all, of KIND is used

blocks.note: a scare = a panic; it goes around the rest
KIND (good) without its last letter

explanation.surface: Alarm over how much good some make-up really does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panic about' looks like a phrase meaning to fret over; 'about' is the container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Skincare is a cosmetic use, the looking after of one's complexion.

clue.text: Really pleasant belting out last bit of sound

indicators.note: the last letter is thrown out

blocks.note: SO NICE, losing its final E

explanation.surface: A singer belting out the last line of a song beautifully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last bit of sound' reads as one phrase; the definition is only 'of sound'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective for adjective: sonic is the Latin-derived word for anything to do with sound, as in sonic boom.

clue.text: Got around boring satellite state

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the letters read backwards
to bore is to drill into something, so these letters go inside the satellite

blocks.note: had = got, obtained; reversed to DAH
Io, a moon of Jupiter; it holds the rest

explanation.surface: Someone who found a satellite dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull; it is drilling into something.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Idaho, in the north-western United States, is one of the fifty states.

clue.text: Mark barrel carried by retired setter repeatedly

indicators.note: BL is held between the two EMs
ME goes backwards, giving EM
the reversed setter appears twice

blocks.note: the setter is ME; reversed
bl = barrel, the trade abbreviation
the second EM

explanation.surface: An old compiler keeps signing a barrel with his mark.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'setter' often means the compiler, ME, as here.
explanation.definitionFit: An emblem is a mark or badge standing for something.

clue.text: Orderly exchange of partners in rear

indicators.note: N and S are partners at bridge, so one is swapped for the other

blocks.note: the seat = the rear, backside; S becomes N

explanation.surface: Swapping dance partners neatly at the back of the hall.
explanation.walkthrough: At bridge North and South play as partners, as do East and West.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a room with everything in its place is both tidy and orderly.

clue.text: Wavering daughter boarding soon?

indicators.note: D gets on board, inside the phrase

blocks.note: in two mins = soon; it holds the D
d = daughter

explanation.surface: A daughter hesitating about getting on a train that leaves shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mins' is the informal short form of minutes, which the question mark covers.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in two minds is to waver, unable to decide.

clue.text: Inattentive fool with note picked up blankets

indicators.note: HEARD covers the E like a blanket

blocks.note: a clot is a fool, in British slang
picked up a sound = heard it; it wraps the E
E, a musical note

explanation.surface: A distracted idiot catching a message about some bedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blankets' looks like a noun for bedding; it is a verb, covers. 'Cloth-eared' is British for bad at listening.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cloth-eared doesn't listen or hear well, so is inattentive.

clue.text: Withdrawn grouch regularly left project

indicators.note: drawn back, so the letters are reversed
every other letter is taken

blocks.note: gRoUcH, the even letters; reversed
L = left

explanation.surface: A sulky grumpy man who dropped out of a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' looks like a scheme; it is the verb, to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: To project something is to throw it forward, to hurl it.
